To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the congruency effect is smaller after incongruent trials than after congruent trials, and that this effect can be found in three different tasks that control for feature binding, contingency learning and response bias.
the congruency effect in three conflict tasks is reduced when preceded by an incongruent trial.
the CSE can occur without feature binding and contingency effects, which suggests that conflict adaptation can account for the CSE.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cognitive control processes involved in the CSE.
the cognitive mechanisms of conflict adaptation, which is a central aspect of the cognitive control system.
the nature of the congruency effects in cognitive control tasks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
conflict adaptation and episodic memory mechanisms are not mutually exclusive, but rather complementary, in explaining the CSE.
the congruency effect is reduced in trials following incongruent ones, and that this effect is due to the fact that incongruent trials are harder and therefore more demanding.
the CSE is not only a function of conflict adaptation but also a function of episodic memory.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CSE can be observed even when feature binding and contingency effects are minimized.
the CSE is a genuine effect of cognitive control, but the exact mechanisms underlying the CSE remain to be further investigated.
the CSE is not a mere by-product of feature binding or contingency learning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CSE can be explained by conflict adaptation, but not in the sense of a general conflict monitor that adjusts attention in all conflict situations.
the notion of conflict monitoring is still the most parsimonious and plausible explanation for the CSE.
the CSE can be obtained in the absence of feature binding or contingency learning and that this finding supports the notion of conflict-driven control adaptation.
